questions.q: Which three founding peoples are the basis of Canada?
questions.e: Canada's three founding peoples are the Aboriginal, French and British.

questions.q: What kind of country is Canada described as?
questions.a: A federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
questions.e: Canada has three defining characteristics: it is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.

questions.q: What are the three main groups of Aboriginal peoples in Canada?
questions.e: There are three distinct groups of Aboriginal peoples: First Nations (once called Indians), Inuit and Métis.

questions.q: Where are the ancestors of Aboriginal peoples believed to have come from many thousands of years ago?
questions.e: The ancestors of Aboriginal peoples are believed to have migrated from Asia many thousands of years ago.

questions.q: Which document of 1763 guaranteed the rights of Aboriginal peoples and set the basis for negotiating treaties?
questions.e: The Royal Proclamation of 1763, issued by King George III, established the basis for negotiating treaties with the newcomers.

questions.q: Which King issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763?
questions.e: King George III issued the Royal Proclamation of 1763, which guaranteed the rights of Aboriginal peoples.

questions.q: What were residential schools?
questions.a: Schools, mostly run by churches and paid for by the federal government, where many Aboriginal children were sent away from their families
w: Schools for children of new immigrants
questions.e: From the 1800s until the 1980s the federal government placed many Aboriginal children in residential schools to educate and assimilate them. The schools were poorly funded and the students suffered hardship and abuse.

questions.q: In which year did the Government of Canada formally apologize to former students of residential schools?
questions.e: In 2008, Ottawa formally apologized to the former students of residential schools.

questions.q: Residential schools operated in Canada from the 1800s until the 1980s.
questions.e: From the 1800s until the 1980s, many Aboriginal children were placed in residential schools, where they were not allowed to speak their languages or practise their culture.

questions.q: Which group makes up the largest part of the Aboriginal population of Canada?
questions.e: About 65% of Aboriginal people are First Nations, about 30% are Métis and about 4% are Inuit.

questions.q: What does the word 'Inuit' mean?
questions.e: Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language.

questions.q: Where do most Inuit live?
questions.a: In small, scattered communities across the Arctic
w: In large cities in southern Ontario
Along the Pacific coast of British Columbia
questions.e: The Inuit live in small, scattered communities across the Arctic. Their knowledge of the land, sea and wildlife helped them adapt to a very harsh environment.

questions.q: Who are the Métis?
questions.a: A distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry
w: Descendants of French settlers in the Maritimes
questions.e: The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry. The majority live in the Prairie provinces.

questions.q: Where do the majority of Métis people live?
questions.e: The Métis come from both French- and English-speaking backgrounds. The majority live in the Prairie provinces.

questions.q: What is the Métis language that mixes French and Aboriginal languages called?
questions.e: The Métis speak their own dialect, Michif.

questions.q: The term 'First Nations' began to be used in the 1970s.
questions.e: 'Indian' refers to all Aboriginal people who are not Inuit or Métis. In the 1970s the term First Nations began to be used.

questions.q: Some First Nations people live on reserve land and others live off-reserve, mainly in cities.
questions.e: About half of First Nations people live on reserve land in about 600 communities, while the other half live off-reserve, mainly in urban centres.

questions.q: Aboriginal and treaty rights are in the Canadian Constitution.
questions.e: Aboriginal and treaty rights are in the Canadian Constitution. Territorial rights were first guaranteed through the Royal Proclamation of 1763.

questions.q: What are the official languages of Canada?
questions.e: English and French are the two official languages and are important symbols of identity.

questions.q: Which Act of 1969 made English and French equal in the federal government?
questions.e: The Official Languages Act (1969) has three main objectives: establishing equality between French and English in Parliament, the federal government and institutions; maintaining and developing official language minority communities; and promoting equality of French and English in Canadian society.

questions.q: Under the Official Languages Act, you have the right to receive federal government services in English or French.
questions.e: The Official Languages Act makes French and English equal in Parliament, the Government of Canada and federal institutions. The public can receive federal services in either language.

questions.q: Who are the Acadians?
questions.a: Descendants of French colonists who began settling in the Maritime provinces in 1604
w: Descendants of Loyalists from the United States
questions.e: The Acadians are the descendants of French colonists who began settling in what are now the Maritime provinces in 1604.

questions.q: What is the deportation of the Acadians between 1755 and 1763 called?
questions.e: Between 1755 and 1763, during the war between Britain and France, more than two-thirds of the Acadians were deported from their homeland. This ethnic cleansing is known as the 'Great Upheaval'.

questions.q: Most Quebecers are descendants of whom?
questions.a: About 8,500 French settlers from the 1600s and 1700s
w: Loyalists who came from the United States
questions.e: The people of Quebec are known as Quebecers. Most are descendants of 8,500 French settlers from the 1600s and 1700s.

questions.q: In 2006, what did the House of Commons recognize?
questions.a: That the Quebecers form a nation within a united Canada
w: That Quebec is a separate country
That French is the only official language
questions.e: In 2006, the House of Commons recognized that the Quebecers form a nation within a united Canada.

questions.q: The English-speaking heritage of Canada comes mainly from settlers from which places?
questions.e: The basic way of life in English-speaking areas was established by hundreds of thousands of English, Welsh, Scottish and Irish soldiers, settlers and immigrants from the 1600s to the 20th century.

questions.q: The Acadians have survived and still keep their unique identity today.
questions.e: Despite the Great Upheaval, the Acadians survived and maintained their unique identity. Today Acadian culture is flourishing.

questions.q: Since the 1970s, where have most immigrants to Canada come from?
questions.e: Since the 1970s, most immigrants have come from Asian countries.

questions.q: After English, which languages are the most spoken at home in two of Canada's biggest cities?
questions.e: Chinese languages are the second most-spoken at home, after English, in two of Canada's biggest cities.

questions.q: What is the largest religious affiliation in Canada?
questions.e: The majority of Canadians identify as Christians. The largest religious affiliation is Catholic, followed by various Protestant churches.

questions.q: Canada is often called a land of immigrants.
questions.e: Over the past 200 years, millions of newcomers have helped to build and defend our way of life. Many ethnic and religious groups live and work in peace as proud Canadians.

questions.q: Being Canadian means you must give up your cultural background.
questions.e: Canadians celebrate diversity. Newcomers can keep their cultural heritage while also respecting Canadian laws and values.

questions.q: Which statement about Canada's diversity is correct?
questions.a: Canadians work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony
w: Only one culture is allowed in Canada
questions.e: Canadians celebrate the gift of one another's presence and work hard to respect pluralism and live in harmony.

questions.q: Many Black Canadians are descendants of Loyalists or of slaves who escaped from the United States.
questions.e: Black Loyalists came to Nova Scotia after the American Revolution, and thousands of slaves escaped from the United States to Canada through the Underground Railroad.

questions.q: Which statement about religion in Canada is correct?
questions.a: Canadians are free to choose their religion, and many faiths live together in peace
w: Everyone must belong to the Catholic Church
Religion is not allowed in public
questions.e: Freedom of conscience and religion is a fundamental freedom. Many religious groups live and work in peace as proud Canadians.

questions.q: The Métis are the Aboriginal people of the Arctic.
questions.e: The Inuit live in the Arctic. The Métis are a distinct people of mixed Aboriginal and European ancestry, mostly in the Prairie provinces.

questions.q: Canada has three official languages: English, French and Inuktitut.
questions.e: Canada has two official languages, English and French. Inuktitut is an official language in Nunavut, not federally.

questions.q: The Acadians are descendants of Loyalists who came from the United States.
questions.e: The Acadians are descendants of French colonists who began settling in the Maritimes in 1604.

questions.q: Aboriginal peoples came to Canada after the first European settlers.
questions.e: The ancestors of Aboriginal peoples lived in Canada for many thousands of years before the Europeans arrived.
